findings.title: Insecure feature gating via unauthenticated query parameter
findings.body: `use_optimized` is derived from a plain client-supplied query parameter (`request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`) with no CSRF/signing protection, and `enable_advanced` relies on `is_superuser` or `has_global_access`. Combined with `OptimizedCursorPaginator`'s negative-offset feature (see paginator.py), this lets any user who happens to have global org access (not necessarily a true superuser) opt into bypassing normal offset bounds. There's no rate limiting or validation that negative offsets stay within sane bounds, so this could be used to scan/exfiltrate audit log entries outside the intended paginated window or cause excessive DB load. At minimum this is an unvetted, security-sensitive code path that should not be toggled by a public query string.

findings.title: Negative offset slicing can return no results or wrap incorrectly, breaking pagination contract
findings.body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset. Django querysets do not support negative indices in slicing (unlike Python lists) — this will raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` at runtime for a real QuerySet, immediately crashing the request instead of gracefully handling pagination. This is also inconsistent with the base `BasePaginator.get_result`, which explicitly clamps `offset` to 0 to avoid this exact issue, suggesting the 'advanced' negative-offset branch was never actually run against a real queryset in testing.

findings.title: Redirect loop depth reduced from 10000 to 1000, lost comment about correctness implications
findings.body: The redirect-chasing loop bound was reduced from 10000 to 1000 without adjusting (or re-validating) the previously documented caveat: 'this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' Reducing the bound to 1000 makes incorrect joins now possible for segment trees of depth >1000 instead of >10000, a significant regression in correctness for deep span trees, and the explanatory comment was deleted so future maintainers won't know why/how this limit interacts with correctness.

findings.title: Changed from a Redis set to sorted set (zset) with eviction, but zunionstore semantics change payload scoring and silently drop spans
findings.body: The script switched from `sadd`/`sunionstore` (plain set semantics, union does not merge/overwrite values) to `zunionstore` using span payloads as members and timestamps as scores. `zunionstore` aggregates scores by default via SUM when the same member exists in both sets, which is likely never intended here (payloads should be unique per span so this may not trigger immediately, but is semantically fragile). More importantly, this change introduces eviction logic in lines 62-64 (`zpopmin` when span_count > 1000) that silently discards the lowest-scored (oldest timestamp) spans once a segment exceeds 1000 members. This is a data-loss change: spans that overflow the limit are silently dropped from the segment rather than being flagged/logged, which will corrupt or truncate large segments without any observability (contrast with the Python-side `_load_segment_data`, which explicitly logs and metrics when max_segment_bytes is exceeded, but the max_segment_spans python-side guard was removed in this PR, see buffer.py diff removing the span-count-exceeded check).

findings.title: Removed max_segment_spans enforcement and error logging on the Python side
findings.body: The diff removes the block that checked `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` and logged/metriced 'segment_span_count_exceeded', deleting the segment from processing with visibility. This safety net is now solely delegated to the new Lua-side zpopmin eviction (add-buffer.lua), which silently drops data with no logging/metrics at all. This is a loss of observability for an already risky operation (truncating a segment), and the `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter is now effectively dead/unused in this file (still accepted as a constructor arg but never enforced), which is misleading to future readers of the code.

findings.title: No test coverage added for new 1000-span eviction behavior
findings.body: The PR title and lua changes introduce span eviction when count exceeds 1000, but no test in test_buffer.py exercises this path (e.g., processing >1000 spans in a segment and asserting that only the most recent 1000 are kept, or that evicted spans are dropped as expected). Given this is a data-dropping behavior change, it should have explicit test coverage verifying the eviction count and which spans are retained/dropped.
